included.title: Sarvam. Open is not sovereign
included.summary: This analysis dissects Sarvam AI, one of India's prominent AI startups, challenging its claims of building sovereign AI technology. The author argues that despite Sarvam's positioning as an Indian AI company focused on local languages and cultural context, its fundamental architecture relies heavily on Western open-source models and infrastructure. The piece explores the tension between 'open' AI development and true technological sovereignty, suggesting that building on open-source foundations from foreign entities doesn't constitute genuine independence. The analysis delves into the technical dependencies that undermine sovereignty claims, from base models to training infrastructure. It raises critical questions about what authentic AI sovereignty looks like in practice versus marketing rhetoric. The author contends that true sovereignty requires building foundational capabilities from the ground up, not just fine-tuning existing Western models for local use cases. This critique extends beyond Sarvam to broader questions about how developing nations can achieve meaningful technological independence in the AI era. The piece serves as a wake-up call for the Indian tech ecosystem about the difference between appearing sovereign and actually being sovereign in AI development.

Buckle up for a masterclass in modern finance's newest vulnerability.

included.title: What's going on with private credit? | Who said what? S2E34
included.summary: The private credit market is experiencing significant turbulence that has industry veterans comparing it to potential systemic risks. Steffen Meister from Partners Group, managing over $180 billion, warned that default rates could double in coming years—a stark assessment that signals deeper structural issues. The article expertly contextualizes private credit's emergence as an alternative to traditional banking, explaining how it fills gaps left by post-2008 regulatory constraints on banks. Unlike traditional lending where banks use short-term deposits for long-term loans, private credit funds match investor capital with borrower needs more directly. However, this shadow banking system now faces stress tests as economic conditions tighten. The piece illuminates how private credit became a $1.7 trillion market by offering higher yields to investors and more flexible terms to borrowers, particularly middle-market companies shut out of public bond markets. But with funds freezing withdrawals and assets being marked down, the sector's rapid growth may have outpaced its risk management capabilities. The analysis reveals how regulatory arbitrage created this parallel lending universe, but also suggests that what goes around comes around—the same market forces that enabled private credit's rise may now threaten its stability.
